AbstractText.Label: PURPOSE
AbstractText.content: Current Children's Oncology Group studies on children with renal malignancy focus on minimizing side effects with a goal of decreasing long term complications. The goal of the present study is to evaluate the patterns of initial imaging in children with renal tumors.

AbstractText.Label: MATERIALS & METHODS
AbstractText.content: We retrospectively reviewed records of 122 patients treated for renal tumors at our institution from 2005 to 2016. Ideal imaging was defined as cross-sectional imaging of C/A/P in one setting without any additional ionizing radiation exposing scans.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Median age of subjects was 33.5mo (range 1-195). Most patients (n=101, 83%) were initially evaluated at an outside facility and subsequently referred to oncology (67.2%) for further workup. Prior to treatment, 58 patients (47.5%) had imaging obtained in an ideal manner. Compared to patients receiving ideal imaging, patients <5yr, 5-9yr, and >10yr received a median additional 2.31mSv (0.9-11.5), 3.08mSv (0.6-11.7), and 5.1mSv (1.2-16) of radiation exposure, respectively. Factors associated with receiving ideal imaging included undergoing abdominal ultrasound (US) as an initial scan (OR=3.637, p=0.001), while presentation to an ER resulted in lower likelihood of receiving ideal imaging (OR=0.351, p=0.012). Factors associated with a lower likelihood of patients receiving initial screening US included presenting with vague symptoms (OR=0.072, p=0.045), and presentation to a tertiary care ER (OR=0.228, p=0.027).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Current patterns of initial imaging for pediatric renal tumors are often associated with unnecessary and avoidable imaging studies. Initial workup with an US scan is associated with a higher likelihood of undergoing ideal imaging, which reduces overall radiation exposure, thus we advocate for an initial abdominal US in all pediatric patients suspected of having an abdominal mass. These data highlight an opportunity for quality improvement across specialties caring for children with renal tumors.

AbstractText.Label: IMPLICATIONS FOR CLINICAL PRACTICE
AbstractText.content: Current investigational priorities for children with renal tumors have shifted to quality improvement and safety with a goal of reduction in treatment-related morbidity. While there is a relatively low risk-benefit ratio for diagnostic imaging in the detection of a potential malignancy, they may contribute to significant toxicities of subsequent therapy via radiation exposure. This study shows that most children with a renal mass did not undergo ideal imaging, resulting in additional ionizing radiation exposure. This is obviously a missed opportunity for providers to efficiently obtain staging information and minimize diagnostic-related morbidity. Furthermore, this is a valuable learning point for physicians who treat these patients, and we encourage starting the workup with an abdominal US. If US demonstrates an abdominal mass concerning for malignancy, this can be followed by staging imaging directed towards the most likely etiology of the tumor. For a renal tumor, we suggest that be cross-sectional imaging of the C/A/P with iv contrast in a single setting to reduce ionizing radiation exposure. Such a work-flow provides the maximal information to all parties involved in caring for the patient while limiting radiation exposure to a child who will likely be exposed to significantly more radiation throughout the course of treatment.
